title: HBr adds Markovnikov: via the more stable carbocation

steps.label: The π bond takes the proton from HBr, giving the 3° carbocation
steps.note: H goes to the CH2 end so the positive charge sits on the carbon with more alkyl groups (3°, not 1°).

steps.label: Bromide attacks the carbocation

why: The C=C π bond is the nucleophile and takes H⁺ from HBr. Putting the H on the CH2 end gives a 3° carbocation (far more stable than the 1° one), and bromide adds there: Markovnikov, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

traps.explains: That's the anti-Markovnikov product, which needs peroxides (a radical chain). Plain HBr goes through the more stable 3° carbocation, so Br ends up on the more substituted carbon.
Two bromines would come from Br2. HBr adds one H and one Br across the C=C.
There's no water here. An OH would need acid-catalysed hydration (H2SO4, H2O); with HBr the nucleophile that captures the cation is bromide.

distractors.explains: Peroxides switch HBr to a radical chain, which puts Br on the CH2 end: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, the anti-Markovnikov product.
Br2 adds two bromines (1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane), not H and Br.

title: HCl addition with a 1,2-hydride shift

steps.label: The π bond takes the proton from HCl, giving a 2° carbocation
steps.note: Markovnikov: H goes to the CH2 end, so the cation is 2°, not 1°.

steps.label: 1,2-Hydride shift: the H on the next carbon moves over with its electrons
steps.note: The 2° cation becomes a more stable 3° cation. Shifts happen whenever a neighbouring H or CH3 can make the cation more stable.

steps.label: Chloride attacks the 3° carbocation

why: Protonation of the C=C gives a 2° carbocation next to a carbon bearing an H. A 1,2-hydride shift turns it into a more stable 3° carbocation before chloride arrives, so Cl ends up on the 3° carbon: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, not 2-chloro-3-methylbutane.

traps.explains: That's the unrearranged product. The 2° carbocation lives long enough for a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable 3° cation, and chloride adds there.
Cl on the end carbon would be anti-Markovnikov. HCl adds H to the CH2 end to make a carbocation, and HCl doesn't do the peroxide (radical) reaction at all.
Losing a proton (E1) is possible, but with chloride present and no heat the cation is captured by Cl⁻. HCl adds; it doesn't just isomerise the alkene.

title: Acid-catalysed hydration: Markovnikov, with a methyl shift

steps.label: The π bond takes a proton from hydronium, giving a 2° carbocation
steps.note: Markovnikov: the H goes to the CH2 end.

steps.label: 1,2-Methyl shift: a CH3 moves over with its bonding electrons
steps.note: The neighbouring carbon has no H, but it has methyls: moving one turns the 2° cation into a 3° cation.

steps.label: Water attacks the 3° carbocation
Another water removes the proton from the oxonium ion
steps.note: Hydronium is regenerated, so the acid is a catalyst.

why: Protonation gives a 2° carbocation next to a quaternary carbon, and a 1,2-methyl shift makes it a more stable 3° cation. Water adds to that carbon and loses a proton, giving 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol. Any reaction that goes through a free carbocation can rearrange like this.

traps.explains: That's the unrearranged Markovnikov alcohol, which oxymercuration–demercuration gives. Acid hydration goes through a free 2° carbocation, and a methyl shift makes it 3° first.
OH on the end carbon is anti-Markovnikov: that's hydroboration–oxidation. Acid puts H on the CH2 end and OH where the cation was.
Dehydration is the reverse reaction, favoured by concentrated acid and heat with water removed. In dilute aqueous acid, the large excess of water pushes the equilibrium toward the alcohol.

distractors.explains: Oxymercuration goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, so nothing rearranges: you get 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, not the 2,3-dimethyl alcohol.
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov and doesn't rearrange: 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.

title: Oxymercuration–demercuration: Markovnikov, no rearrangement
why: Hg(OAc)⁺ adds to the C=C as a bridged mercurinium ion, so there is never a free carbocation and nothing rearranges. Water opens the bridge at the more substituted carbon (it holds more δ+), and NaBH4 then replaces Hg with H: Markovnikov 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.

traps.explains: That's the rearranged alcohol from H2SO4/H2O, which goes through a free carbocation. The mercurinium ion is bridged, so no methyl shift happens.
OH on the end carbon is anti-Markovnikov (hydroboration–oxidation). Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the mercurinium ion.
That's the organomercury intermediate after step 1. Step 2 (NaBH4) replaces the C–Hg bond with C–H.

distractors.explains: Acid hydration goes through a free 2° carbocation, which undergoes a methyl shift: 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov: OH ends up on the CH2 (3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol).

review: No mechanism card: the NaBH4 demercuration step is a radical process that the arrow simulator can't draw, and a mechanism has to end at the product. The key step shown is water opening the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon; the mercurinium is drawn as a three-membered ring with Hg⁺ bonded to one acetate. Please check that depiction.

title: Hydroboration–oxidation: anti-Markovnikov alcohol

steps.label: BH3 adds across the C=C in one step: B to the less substituted carbon, H to the other
steps.note: Concerted four-centre step, so B and H add to the same face (syn) and no carbocation forms. Each BH3 really adds to three alkenes; one is drawn.

steps.label: Hydroxide deprotonates hydrogen peroxide
The hydroperoxide anion attacks the empty p orbital on boron
The alkyl group moves from boron to oxygen as hydroxide leaves
steps.note: The carbon keeps its configuration as it moves (retention), so OH ends up exactly where B was.

steps.label: Hydroxide adds to boron
The B–O bond breaks, releasing the alkoxide
Water protonates the alkoxide

why: Boron is the electrophile and goes to the less hindered CH2 end, while H goes to the inner carbon, in one concerted step with no carbocation (so no rearrangement). Oxidation swaps C–B for C–OH, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.

traps.explains: That's the Markovnikov alcohol from oxymercuration–demercuration. In hydroboration, boron (and so the OH) goes to the less substituted carbon.
A methyl shift needs a carbocation. Hydroboration is a concerted four-centre addition, so nothing rearranges; this product comes from H2SO4/H2O.
H2O2/NaOH replaces the C–B bond with C–OH and stops there. An aldehyde would need a separate oxidation (e.g. PCC).

distractors.explains: Acid hydration is Markovnikov and the 2° cation rearranges: 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Oxymercuration is Markovnikov: OH goes on the inner carbon (3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol).

title: Hydroboration–oxidation: syn addition on a ring

steps.label: BH3 adds across the C=C in one step: B to the less substituted carbon, H to the other
steps.note: Concerted four-centre step, so B and H add to the same face (syn) and no carbocation forms. Each BH3 really adds to three alkenes; one is drawn.

steps.label: Hydroxide deprotonates hydrogen peroxide
The hydroperoxide anion attacks the empty p orbital on boron
The alkyl group moves from boron to oxygen as hydroxide leaves
steps.note: The carbon keeps its configuration as it moves (retention), so OH ends up exactly where B was.

steps.label: Hydroxide adds to boron
The B–O bond breaks, releasing the alkoxide
Water protonates the alkoxide

why: B and H add to the same face in one step: B to the less substituted CH, H to the carbon with the methyl. Oxidation replaces B with OH with retention, so OH and the new H are cis, which puts OH trans to the methyl: trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (racemic: ±, both faces react equally).

traps.explains: That's cis-2-methylcyclohexanol, which would need anti addition. B and H add to the same face (syn), and OH replaces B with retention, so OH ends up trans to the CH3.
OH on the carbon with the methyl is the Markovnikov product (H2SO4/H2O or oxymercuration). Boron goes to the less substituted carbon.
H2O2/NaOH swaps the boron for OH. Replacing B with H would need a carboxylic acid (protonolysis), not peroxide.

title: Br2 addition: anti, through a bromonium ion

steps.label: The π bond attacks Br2; Br⁻ leaves and the near Br bridges both carbons
steps.note: The bridged bromonium ion has no free carbocation, so there is no rearrangement, and it blocks one face.

steps.label: Bromide attacks a ring carbon from the back side, opening the bromonium ion
steps.note: Backside (SN2-like) attack puts the two bromines on opposite faces: anti addition.

why: Br2 forms a bridged bromonium ion on one face of the ring, so bromide has to attack from the opposite face. Anti addition to cyclohexene gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane (racemic: ±), never the cis isomer.

traps.explains: That's cis-1,2-dibromocyclohexane, which would need syn addition. The bromonium ion blocks one face, so Br⁻ attacks from the other: anti, giving trans.
Bromocyclohexane is the HBr product (H and Br). Br2 adds a bromine to each alkene carbon.
Substitution at the allylic position is the radical reaction (NBS, light). Br2 in CH2Cl2 in the dark adds across the C=C.

title: Bromohydrin: OH on the more substituted carbon, anti

steps.label: The π bond attacks Br2, forming a bromonium ion
Water attacks the more substituted carbon from the back side
steps.note: Water is the solvent, so it far outnumbers Br⁻. The C–Br bond to the 3° carbon is longer and that carbon holds more δ+, so water goes there.

steps.label: Another water removes the proton from the oxonium ion

why: Br2 forms a bromonium ion, and water (the solvent, in huge excess) opens it from the back face at the more substituted carbon, which carries more positive charge. So OH goes on the 3° carbon, Br on the 2° carbon, and they end up trans: trans-2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (racemic: ±).

traps.explains: That's the cis bromohydrin, which would need syn addition. Water attacks the bromonium ion from the face opposite Br, so OH and Br are trans.
The regiochemistry is reversed. Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bromonium ion (more δ+), so OH goes on the carbon with the methyl.
The dibromide forms in CH2Cl2. Here water is the solvent and outnumbers bromide, so water opens the bromonium ion.

title: mCPBA epoxidation: syn and stereospecific

steps.label: One concerted step: the π bond attacks the outer O, the O–O bond breaks, and the C=O takes the proton
steps.note: Both C–O bonds form on the same face at the same time, so the alkene's geometry is kept: cis-alkene → cis-epoxide.

why: The peroxyacid delivers one O to both alkene carbons from the same face in a single concerted step, so the geometry of the alkene is kept. cis-2-Butene gives cis-2,3-dimethyloxirane (a meso compound); trans-2-butene would give the trans epoxide.

traps.explains: That's trans-2,3-dimethyloxirane, from trans-2-butene. Epoxidation is concerted and syn, so the cis groups stay cis.
Opening the epoxide to a diol needs a second step (H3O+). mCPBA in CH2Cl2 stops at the epoxide.
No hydrogen moves to make a ketone. The O bridges both carbons that were in the C=C.

title: OsO4: syn dihydroxylation
why: OsO4 adds both oxygens to the same face in one concerted step, forming a cyclic osmate ester. Cleaving the Os–O bonds (NaHSO3, H2O) leaves the C–O bonds untouched, so both OH groups are cis: cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol (meso).

traps.explains: That's trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, the anti product of epoxidation then H3O+. OsO4 delivers both oxygens from the same face.
The epoxide comes from a peroxyacid (mCPBA). OsO4 gives a diol with an OH on each carbon.
Breaking the C=C completely needs ozonolysis or hot, acidic KMnO4. OsO4 (or cold, dilute KMnO4) keeps the C–C bond and adds two OH groups.

distractors.explains: Epoxide opening by water is backside (anti), so this gives trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, not the cis diol.
Ozonolysis breaks the C=C completely, giving hexanedial.

review: No mechanism card: hydrolysis of the cyclic osmate ester (NaHSO3, H2O) isn't a clean textbook arrow sequence. The key step is the concerted [3+2] addition drawn as four arrows (π bond → O, other O's lone pair → C, both Os=O π bonds back onto Os/O, giving an Os(VI) osmate ester). Please check this depiction; the cold KMnO4 aliases are listed as accepted alternatives.

title: Epoxide then H3O+: anti dihydroxylation

steps.label: mCPBA transfers an O to the C=C in one concerted step, giving the epoxide
Step 2: hydronium protonates the epoxide oxygen
Water attacks a ring carbon from the back side as the C–O bond breaks
steps.note: Backside attack: the new OH comes in on the face opposite the old epoxide oxygen.

steps.label: Water removes the proton from the oxonium ion

why: The epoxide O is on one face of the ring. In acid, water opens the protonated epoxide by backside attack, so the second OH comes in on the opposite face: anti addition overall, trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol (racemic: ±). Compare OsO4, which gives the cis diol.

traps.explains: That's cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, the syn product of OsO4. Water opens the epoxide from the back side, so the two OH groups end up trans.
That's where step 1 stops. Step 2 (H3O+) opens the epoxide to the diol.
Cyclohexanol is the hydration product (H and OH). Here each alkene carbon ends up with an oxygen.

distractors.explains: OsO4 adds both oxygens to the same face: cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, not trans.
Bromine water gives the trans bromohydrin (one OH, one Br), not a diol.

title: Ozonolysis: cut the C=C, make two C=O
why: Ozone cleaves the C=C completely and each alkene carbon becomes a C=O. Because the C=C is in a ring, the ring opens into one chain: the carbon with the methyl becomes a ketone and the CH becomes an aldehyde. DMS (reductive workup) keeps the aldehyde from being oxidised: 5-oxohexanal.

traps.explains: The carboxylic acid forms with an oxidative workup (H2O2) or hot KMnO4. Dimethyl sulfide is a reducing workup, so the aldehyde survives.
The epoxide comes from mCPBA, which keeps the C–C bond. Ozone breaks both bonds of the C=C.
The diol comes from OsO4 or cold KMnO4. Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C into two carbonyls.

distractors.explains: An oxidative workup turns the aldehyde into a carboxylic acid: 5-oxohexanoic acid.
Hot, acidic permanganate also cleaves the C=C but oxidises the aldehyde end to COOH.

title: Catalytic hydrogenation: syn addition of H2
why: Both hydrogens are delivered from the metal surface to the same face of the C=C (syn addition). The two methyls get pushed to the other face together, so 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene gives cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane (meso).

traps.explains: That's trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, which would need anti addition. The alkene lies flat on the catalyst and both H atoms add from below: syn.
Nothing migrates. There is no carbocation; each alkene carbon simply gains one H.
There is no water or acid. Hydrogenation adds H–H across the C=C; an OH would need hydration.

title: HBr with peroxides: anti-Markovnikov (radical)
why: Peroxides start a radical chain: Br• (not H⁺) adds first, to the CH2 end, so the more stable 3° radical forms on the inner carbon. That radical takes H from HBr, so H ends on the more substituted carbon and Br on the end: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. Only HBr does this; HCl and HI don't.

traps.explains: That's the Markovnikov product of HBr without peroxides (via the carbocation). With peroxides, Br• adds first and goes to the CH2 end.
Two bromines come from Br2. HBr adds one H and one Br.
Substitution at the allylic CH3 is NBS chemistry (low Br2, light). With HBr and peroxides, H and Br add across the C=C.
